slides.title: New Primitives For Euclidean Geometry
slides.notes: Open by framing the chapter as a change in the unit of computation. The conformal model does not merely add another coordinate trick; it lets points, point pairs, circles, spheres, flats, rounds, and tangents enter the same product language. Ask students to watch how incidence data and probe equations become two views of one primitive vocabulary.

slides.title: Primitive Roster
slides.notes: Use this roster to settle terminology before formulas accumulate. A point is a null vector, a flat carries infinity, a round has finite squared size, and a tangent is the zero-size round with a direction attached. The visual point is that these are not separate data structures; they are blade families with different tests.

slides.title: Point Lift And Probe
slides.notes: Emphasize the dual role of the lifted point. It is a null vector encoding location, but it also makes distance into an inner product. Once students accept that a point can probe another point, the same act of probing a dual sphere naturally returns power, incidence, and signed inside-outside information.

slides.title: Direct Rounds From Data
slides.notes: Read the slide from left to right as a data workflow. Two measured points produce a point pair, three noncollinear points produce a circle, and four noncoplanar points produce a sphere. The direct blade is best when observations define the object; parameter recovery is a later operation rather than the original representation.

slides.title: Dual Rounds As Probes
slides.notes: Now reverse the direction of use. A center-radius description is most useful as a dual object because a point can test itself against it by one inner product. Highlight that the sign of the power value is meaningful: on-shell is zero, outside is positive, and inside is negative for the displayed convention.

slides.title: Direct And Dual Forms
slides.notes: The slide is a map for choosing a representation, not a demand to memorize signs. Direct form fits incidence construction, while dual form fits testing, fitting, and intersections expressed through dual meets. The carrier flat keeps orientation visible, and infinity tells the algebra whether a primitive is flat or round.

slides.title: Tangents Are Zero-Size Rounds
slides.notes: Use the three panels as a continuity argument. The same two-sphere meet passes from a real circle, to a zero-radius contact, to an imaginary circle. Tangents are therefore not infinitesimal exceptions; they are finite conformal elements whose squared size is zero while their weight and direction can remain nonzero.

slides.title: Classifying Blades
slides.notes: This is the operational checklist behind the long table in the chapter. First ask whether infinity is contained or contracted away, then ask whether the square vanishes, and finally decide whether the blade is being interpreted directly or dually. The tests let software route an unknown result to the right drawing and parameter recovery path.

slides.title: Representative Paraboloid
slides.notes: The paraboloid is only a visualization of part of the conformal model, but it is extremely useful. Lifted Euclidean points sit on the graph, a point determines a tangent plane, and a dual circle appears as an affine plane cutting the graph. The ordinary circle is the shadow of that plane section.

slides.title: Intersections Become Linear
slides.notes: Make the key simplification explicit. In Euclidean coordinates, intersecting circles looks quadratic. In the conformal lift, the same circles are represented by planes, so their meet is a line. Where that line cuts the paraboloid we recover a point pair; if it misses, the algebra still reports an imaginary pair.

slides.title: Incidence And Meet Tests
slides.notes: Treat these as small diagnostics students can implement. Point-on-round is an inner-product residual, point-pair extraction is a factorization step, and intersection uses a meet or dual meet depending on representation. The important habit is to keep a numeric residual or sign test next to every geometric claim.

slides.title: Power, Voronoi, Delaunay
slides.notes: Connect the chapter to computational geometry. Ordinary Voronoi cells compare squared distances, while power diagrams compare squared distance minus radius squared. The paraboloid lift explains why the boundaries are linear after cancellation, and duality explains why the Delaunay triangulation appears as the convex hull of lifted sites.

slides.title: Fitting Spheres And Planes
slides.notes: The fitting example shows the practical value of dual rounds. Noisy points become rows in a linear algebra problem, and the smallest singular direction gives the dual primitive. A plane is not a failure here; it is the conformal answer when the best sphere has moved through infinity.

slides.title: Kinematics From Sphere Meets
slides.notes: Use the arm as an application of the same classification from the tangent slide. The shoulder link says the elbow lies on one sphere, and the hand link says it lies on another. Their meet is a circle, a tangent point, or an imaginary circle, corresponding exactly to reachable, limiting, or unreachable targets.

slides.title: Carry Forward
slides.notes: Close with the modeling message. Chapter 14 is less about collecting exotic objects than about reducing casework. Once circles, spheres, point pairs, flats, rounds, dual forms, and tangents are native blades, later construction algorithms can combine probing, fitting, transformation, and intersection without leaving the conformal algebra.
